title: Tenant-specific Terraform patterns for Private VPC customization and safe upgrades
creator: Aisha Ramos
description:
Problem: Customers deploying Redwood Private into their VPCs need a predictable, supportable way to customize Terraform without forking core modules. Current patterns (ad-hoc overlays, per-customer repo forks) create drift, upgrade pain, and slow support. This ticket defines recommended, practical patterns for tenant-specific Terraform customization, upgrade hooks, and health-check automation that balance customer flexibility with maintainability and safe upgrades.

Goals:
- Provide a small set of supported customization primitives (overlays, variable maps, composition shims) customers can use without modifying core modules.
- Standardize an upgrade hook pattern so operator teams can run canary upgrades and automated sanity checks before wide rollouts.
- Define health-check integration so a failed post-upgrade smoke test triggers automatic rollback/fallback.
- Reduce per-customer drift by enabling composition via wrapper modules and thin overlay layers.

Recommended patterns (summary):
1) Composition-first modules: publish core modules to our private Terraform Registry. Core modules are strictly inputs-driven and expose small, well-documented extension points (input maps, locals to merge). Customers compose these modules via short wrapper modules (tenant_<name>_overlay) in their tenant repos. Wrapper modules only set vars and call core modules—they do not copy core logic.

2) Overlay shims using locals.merge: encourage overlays that pass a single map var (custom_overrides) which gets merged with defaults inside the core module using a documented locals.merge pattern. This keeps defaults in core modules and lets customers override only keys they need. Example: var custom_subnets = map(string) and locals { final_subnets = merge(var.default_subnets, var.custom_subnets) }

3) Feature gates via structured variables: rather than Boolean flags scattered across modules, expose a single var feature_flags = { key = true } so customer-level toggles remain declarative and centrally auditable.

4) Tenant patch modules: allow small, versioned "patch" modules in a dedicated namespace (redwood/tenant-patches) that reference core modules and apply cross-cutting tenant adjustments (e.g., tag normalization, route table tweaks). Patch modules are short lived and versioned so upgrades can drop the patch when upstream supports the capability.

5) Remote state & backends: recommend one state per-tenant environment (prod/stage) with DynamoDB locking and S3 (or equivalent) remote backend. Document how customers can use workspace namespacing for short-lived dev work but avoid long-term workspaces for prod.

6) Upgrade hooks and canary workflow: introduce a standard pattern where the tenant repo exposes two targets: apply-canary and apply-rollout. The operator CI runs: terraform plan (canary) -> terraform apply (canary) -> run post-deploy healthchecks; if green, automatically trigger rollout pipeline. Healthchecks are implemented as a separate job that calls an endpoint and verifies token-level responses and latency SLOs.

7) Post-upgrade healthcheck strategy: define a small, composable healthcheck suite per tenant that can run as part of the upgrade pipeline. Healthchecks are stored as JSON/YAML in the tenant repo (not in core modules) and executed by our upgrade runner. Include: endpoint probe, token flow test, and a lightweight RL (request/response) correctness check. Failure should trigger an automated rollback plan (apply previous state) and open a remediation ticket automatically.

8) Plan-only gating & plan diffs: CI must publish plan diffs into console dashboards. For customer-facing upgrades, require an approver for changes that touch networking, IAM, or storage. Provide a script that extracts a compact diff summary for reviewers.

9) Version pinning and compatibility ranges: recommend using explicit module versions with semver ranges in tenant wrapper modules. Core modules must document breaking changes in a UPGRADE.md and provide migration helpers.

Implementation notes and trade-offs:
- Pros: wrapper/overlay approach minimizes code duplication and makes upgrades tractable; standard hooks enable safe canaries and automated remediation.
- Cons: an extra wrapper layer increases indirection; customers must adopt the pattern which may require conversion scripts for existing forks.
- Trade-offs: Allowing patch modules gives immediate ergonomics, but we limit their scope and lifetime to avoid permanent drift.

Operational considerations:
- Provide a migration tool to convert a forked repo into a wrapper + patch module layout; include automated diff checks.
- Build CI templates that customers can drop in: plan-only, apply-canary, healthcheck, apply-rollout, rollback.
- We must validate module inputs server-side in our onboarding checks to prevent unsafe network modifications (e.g., changing routes to public subnets).

Examples (practical snippets):
- Wrapper module example: tenant-network/main.tf that calls registry module redwood/vpc/core with custom_overrides var and sets feature_flags.
- Upgrade hook: use a small runner job that records pre-upgrade state, tags the previous module version in a release branch, runs canary apply, runs healthchecks, and either triggers rollout or rolls back via stored plan.

Acceptance criteria (see list):
- Proposal documented in Private-Deployment-Modernization repo
- CI templates and runner library implemented and tested against 2 tenant sandboxes
- Migration helper script implemented and validated on at least two customer forks
- Healthcheck runner integrated with console and alerting
- UPGRADE.md added to core modules describing migration paths for breaking changes

Out of scope for this ticket: automated UI for patch modules, marketplace onboarding flow, and custom onboarding workshops (these can be follow-ups).
acceptance_criteria: Pattern docs checked into private-deployment repo with examples
CI templates (plan, canary, rollout, rollback) committed and exercised in staging
Migration helper script (fork->wrapper) produces idempotent wrapper conversion and a report
Healthcheck runner executes declared JSON/YAML suites and integrates result into console metrics
Core modules include UPGRADE.md and explicit semver guidance

notes: Prefer merge patterns over copy-paste for maintainability
Patch modules should be timeboxed in their README with sunset criteria
Healthchecks must include both availability and basic output sanity checks
Limit the number of exposed knobs on core modules to avoid combinatorial complexity
